A company stores backups in an Amazon S3 bucket. The backups must not be deleted for at least 3 months after they are created.  
  
What should a CloudOps engineer do to satisfy this requirement?

options.text: Configure an IAM policy that denies the s3:DeleteObject action for all users. Three months after an object is written, remove the policy.
Enable S3 Object Lock on a new S3 bucket in compliance mode. Place all backups in the new S3 bucket with a retention period of 3 months.
Enable S3 Versioning on the existing S3 bucket. Configure S3 Lifecycle rules to protect the backups.
Enable S3 Object Lock on a new S3 bucket in governance mode. Place all backups in the new S3 bucket with a retention period of 3 months.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 Object Lock in compliance mode provides write-once-read-many (WORM) protection: a retained object version cannot be deleted or overwritten before its retention period expires. A three-month retention period therefore enforces the required minimum retention, whereas governance mode can be bypassed by a principal granted the appropriate permission.

**Learn more:** [Locking objects with Object Lock - Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html) · [Configuring S3 Object Lock - Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock-configure.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company keeps critical data in an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. During peak shopping hours, the company observes degraded performance, high CPU utilization, greater query latency, and connection timeouts. The company also detects spikes in user connections during those peak periods. These connection spikes affect the database's read performance.  
  
The company needs to resolve the database performance problems.  
  
Which combination of steps will meet this requirement? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use Amazon RDS Performance Insights to analyze the SQL queries that most affect database performance. Update the SQL queries based on the analysis findings.
Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to analyze the database queries and identify performance bottlenecks. Update the queries based on the analysis findings.
Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a single Availability Zone.
Disable connection pooling entirely to ensure that all user connections are treated equally, even during peak hours.
Implement RDS Proxy with connection pooling.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS Performance Insights provides database-load visibility by SQL and identifies the top SQL queries contributing to load, enabling query tuning to reduce CPU and latency. Amazon RDS Proxy establishes and reuses a connection pool, allowing applications to share database connections and handle unpredictable traffic surges without creating excessive direct database connections.

**Learn more:** [Analyzing queries with the Top SQL tab in Performance Insights](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_PerfInsights.UsingDashboard.AnalyzeDBLoad.AdditionalMetrics.html) · [Amazon RDS Proxy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company uses an AWS Organizations organization to manage a multi-account AWS environment. The company creates a new Amazon EBS-backed Amazon Machine Image (AMI) and shares the AMI across the organization. Employees must use the AMI to launch all new Linux-based Amazon EC2 instances throughout the organization.  
  
In one of the company’s application accounts, an employee uses the new AMI to launch a workload. The EC2 instance launches but is terminated immediately.  
  
What is the **MOST** likely reason the instance did not fully boot?

options.text: The user who launched the instance does not have ec2:RunInstances permissions within the application account.
The company encrypted the AMI by using an AWS KMS key that the user who launched the EC2 instance does not have access to.
There is a service control policy (SCP) that denies the user who launched the EC2 instance access to launch instances in the application account.
The user launched the EC2 instance into a subnet that does not have access to the internet.

questions.explanation:
When an AMI is backed by encrypted EBS snapshots and shared with an AWS Organization, the KMS key that encrypted those snapshots must also permit the consuming principals or accounts to use it. Without access to that key, EC2 cannot use the encrypted root volume needed for the instance to boot.

**Learn more:** [Allow organizations and OUs to use a KMS key](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/allow-org-ou-to-use-key.html) · [Manage AMI sharing with an organization or OU](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/share-amis-org-ou-manage.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company operates on-premises workloads that must use AWS-hosted DNS services. The company needs highly available DNS queries to provide uninterrupted DNS resolution for critical applications.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy Amazon Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints to multiple Availability Zones. Configure on-premises DNS resolvers to use the endpoint IP addresses in a failover configuration.
Use Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to ensure that DNS queries from on-premises systems are directed to the closest resolver endpoint.
Configure an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone. Associate the private hosted zone with the on-premises network.
Deploy Amazon Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints to multiple Availability Zones. Associate the endpoints with the on-premises DNS resolvers.

questions.explanation:
A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint accepts DNS queries from on-premises DNS resolvers and forwards them to the VPC Resolver. Using endpoint IP addresses in multiple Availability Zones provides redundancy, and configuring the on-premises resolvers to fail over between those IP addresses maintains DNS resolution if an endpoint or Availability Zone becomes unavailable.

**Learn more:** [High availability for Resolver endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/best-practices-resolver-endpoint-high-availability.html) · [Forwarding inbound DNS queries to your VPCs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-forwarding-inbound-queries.html)
